title: 684530455242/541NV17: Newgale House, Newgale, Haverfordwest, SA62 6AS
text:
TRIBIWNLYS PRISIO CYMRU  -  VALUATION TRIBUNAL FOR WALES

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 1 of 10

Appellant:  Gengard Ltd

Appeal property: Newgale House, Newgale, Haverfordwest

Appeal number: 684530455242/541NV17

The Matter Appealed against: Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Date of Hearing: 3rd September 2019

Appearances: Mr M Carter (for Gengard Ltd) & Mrs S Harris (for respondent
Valuation Officer)

Date of Decision: 30th September 2019

Decision of Tribunal: Allowed (in part) Rateable Value £14,500 with effect
from 1st April 2017

Members of the Tribunal: Mrs C A Green (Chairperson), Mr N R J Edwards
& Mrs B C Martin

Tribunal Clerk: Mr J Evans

Introduction

1. On 31st January 2018, the Valuation Officer (VO) received a proposal
which challenged the alteration that was made to the Rating List in respect
of the appeal property Newgale House, Newgale. The proposal was made
by Mr M Carter for the appellant company “Gengard Ltd” who occupied the
property that was the subject of this appeal.

2. In making the proposal for Gengard Ltd, Mr Carter sought a reduction in
the revised Rateable Value of £17,250 with effect from 1st April 2017 to
Rateable Value £7,500.

3. Since the VO did not agree to alter the list to the extent Mr Carter sought
for in the proposal, the matter was remitted to the Valuation Tribunal for
Wales according to Regulation of the Non-Domestic Rating (Alteration of
List and Appeals) (Wales) Regulations 2005, as amended.

4. This is a summary of the case and is not intended to be an exhaustive
record of the proceedings. However, the parties can be assured that all the
evidence was fully considered by the tribunal when it arrived at its
decision. Consequently, the absence of reference to any statement, or
evidence, should not be construed as being overlooked.

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 2 of 10
Summary of the Case

5. As is customary in cases of this nature where the proposal challenged the
Valuation Officer’s Notice, Mrs Harris was invited to present the Valuation
Officer’s case first.

6. In her opening statement, Mrs Harris pointed out that she represented the
Valuation Officer for Wales in a dual role of advocate and expert witness.

7. In her role as advocate, Mrs Harris explained how the proposal came to be
made and, with reference to its Parts B (details of the Proposed List
Alteration) and C (Grounds for your proposed alteration), she set out the
parameters and scope of the issues that were under appeal.

8. Mrs Harris then referred to Paragraph 2 (1), Schedule 6 of the Local
Government Finance Act 1988 (the Act) which set out the definition of
Rateable Value for these purposes. The extract Mrs Harris referred to
stated –

The rateable value of a non-domestic hereditament … shall be taken to
be an amount equal to the rent at which it is estimated the
hereditament might reasonably be expected to let from year to year on
these three assumptions;

a. the first assumption is that the tenancy begins on the day by
reference to which the determination is to be made;

b. the second assumption is that immediately before the tenancy
begins the hereditament is in a state of reasonable repair, but
excluding from this assumption any repairs which a reasonable
landlord would consider uneconomic;

c. the third assumption is that the tenant undertakes to pay all usual
tenant’s rates and taxes and to bear the cost of the repairs and
insurance and the other expenses (if any) necessary to maintain the
hereditament in a state to command the rent mentioned above.

9. With reference to the Rating Lists (Valuation Date) (Wales) Order 2014
[the Valuation Date], Mrs Harris pointed out that 1st April 2015 was the day
by reference to which the rateable values of non-domestic hereditaments
are to be determined for the purposes of the local and central non-
domestic rating lists which are compiled for Wales on 1st April 2017.

10. In considering the appellant’s case, Mrs Harris had regard to the principles
established in Lotus and Delta v Culverwell (VO) [1976] an extract of
which was referred to earlier in her submission. She said that these
principles suggested that the weight to be given to a rent depended on
how closely it complied with the statutory definition of Rateable Value.

Page 3 of 10
11. In her expert witness statement, Mrs Harris described the appeal property
and with the aim of maps and plans she identified its location and
amenities. The property comprised a ground floor shop with residential
accommodation to the upper floor and had a total non-domestic area of
322.43m2. An inspection of the property was undertaken on 11th
December 2017. Her schedule of evidence included a location plan, a
layout plan of the appeal property; images of the appeal property; rental
evidence; assessment evidence and her valuation of the property under
consideration.

12. Mrs Harris explained that Newgale House was entered into the compiled
2017 Rating List at Rateable Value £18,750 with effect from 1st April 2017.
This was amended to £17,250 based on a revised measurement of its
area with effect from 1st April 2017.

13. In reviewing the rateable value for Newgale House, Mrs Harris had regard
to agreements reached in respect of two other properties in the area:
“Newsurf” and “Sands Café”.

14. Mrs Harris said that Newsurf was a surfing retail outlet that offered both
new and used surf equipment, on site surf hire, surfboard repairs and
surfing instruction.

15. The property resembled a house in built appearance and like Newgale
House it has a non-standard frontage. It is occupied as a shop with stores.
It comprised a total area of 251.88 m2 but in terMrs of its main space
(ITMRS), it had an area of 211.44m2. Mrs Harris explained that the

18. Mrs Harris explained that the agreements made on these properties with
the respective ratepayers underpinned her revised valuation for the appeal
property. As a corollary she advanced an underlying level of value of
£55.00/m2 which she considered reflected its size and age; she applied an
end allowance for structural walls and a staircase which were located at
the front of the property. Her revised valuation for the subject property was
Rateable Value £14,500 with effect from 1st April 2017 which she said was
offered to Mr Carter in advance of the hearing.

19. Mrs Harris said that during the course of preparing and serving the
requisite documents on Mr Carter, she received an email from Mr
Sanderson who was the appellant ratepayer of two of the three properties

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 5 of 10
she cited in her submission. Mr Sanderson informed her that he wished to
make subsequent proposals because he felt the rateable value was too
high. Mr Sanderson also pointed out that he did not wish Gengard’s
appeal to be “distorted by false facts” and maintained that he remained
unhappy with the valuation he had been given. In her response, Mrs Harris
explained that Mr Sanderson had formally settled his rating appeal with the
VO on 28th April 2019. However, in light of comments Mr Sanderson had
made more recently, Mrs Harris pointed out that the rating regime did not
permit one to make a second proposal on the same grounds as the first. In
support of this, she referred to Regulation 4 (3) (b) (i) of the Non-Domestic
Rating (Alteration of Lists and Appeals) (Wales) Regulations 2005 -

(3) No proposal may be made —
(b) by an interested person, where —
(i) that person (or a person having a qualifying connection with that
person) has made a proposal to alter the same list in relation to the
same hereditament on the same ground and arising from the same
event;
20. In response to questions from Mr Carter, Mrs Harris said that the
circuMrstances he had referred to in his case about matters affecting the
integrity of the coastline in Newgale had occurred prior to the Antecedent
Valuation date of 1st April 2015. Consequently, such matter would have
been taken into account during the course of the 2017 Rating revaluation.

21. Mrs Harris acknowledged that the RV for the 2017 Rating List was
considerably higher than that attributed to the 2010 list entry. However,
she pointed out that the two lists were underpinned by different underlying
levels of values which were brought about by differing economic
circuMrstances: 1st April 2008 for the 2010 Rating Revaluation and 1st April
2015 in respect of the one currently in force.

23. In her appendices, Mrs Mrs Harris referred to a “Notice of Information to
Be Used in Evidence” document in respect of Sands Café, Newgale.

24. In view of the foregoing, Mrs Harris asked the Tribunal to confirm her
revised valuation of the subject property of £14,500 with effect from 1st
April 2017.

25. In his opening remarks, Mr Carter referred to a report which was
presented at a valuation tribunal hearing in which he contended that the
RV attributed to his 2010 rating appeal was excessive. The same report
was used by the appellant in the matter now under consideration. The
author of this report, Mr Andrew Parr, was a chartered surveyor with
extensive experience of some 35 years in the letting of commercial
property in the Haverfordwest area. Unfortunately, Mr Parr was unable to
accompany Mr Carter to the hearing of his 2017 rating appeal.
Nevertheless, this report was placed before the Tribunal for its
consideration.

26. Mr Carter referred to the substantial increase in the appeal property’s
valuation that came about as a result of the 2017 Non-Domestic
Revaluation. He said that despite the substantial increase in the Valuation
Officer’s valuation of the appeal property, no explanation had been
received.

27. Mr Carter explained that for the past ten years, Newgale had featured in
the Shoreline Management Plan and was a designated “managed retreat
area”. It was also situated in a C2 and C3 flood risk area. In January 2014
a freak wave hit a bus as it drove through Newgale along the A487. The
A487 trunk road runs through Newgale and past the subject property. Mr
Carter explained that the bus sustained significant damage having been
swept from the road as a result of the severity of the wave. As a corollary,
Pembrokeshire County Council (PCC) conducted a thorough study of the
shingle bank in Newgale where its conclusions about the foregoing were
made public on 23rd February 2015.

28. As a result of its findings, PCC cast considerable doubt upon continued
maintenance of the shingle bank that had protected the road for more than
ten years. As there would be an impact to the position of the road the
authority planned to divert the A487 and allow the sea to come inland.
Although a number of options about how this should be done were
explored, the preferred outcome was to take the road away from Newgale
which left a dead end outside the appeal property. Other choices involved
making a new road that went straight through the position on which the
appeal property was situated and led to the creation of a causeway over
the headland. Mr Carter had not been persuaded that the VOA had taken
factors such as this into account which he believed would have influenced
rental values during the course of the 2017 Non-Domestic Revaluation.

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 7 of 10
29. With regard to the appeal property, Mr Carter said that he and a
consortium of others (Mr D M Carter and Mr G James) purchased the
appeal property in 1995. The occupier and trading company was Gengard
Ltd. Upon the death of Mr D Carter, Mr Carter’s (appellant) share in the
property was increased from 39% to 83%. A rental arrangement was
introduced which involved the lease of the downstairs building to Gengard
Ltd for £7,500 per annum. On 1st December 2017, a long-term rental
agreement came into force for the same amount which was assumed
under advisement from Mr Parr. Gengard is owned by Mark, David, Amy
and Meryl Carter and Mr James. Messrs Carter (Mark and David) are
employed by Gengard Ltd. Mr Carter explained that the VO was fully
aware of this arrangement but had chosen not to mention this at the
previous hearing. The upstairs accommodation was used as domestic
accommodation and subject to council tax.

30. Mr Carter said that the “Carter” family owned and operated the ‘Sands’
Café from approximately 1988. It was initially leased to a local family and
then to the current owner. The Café fronted the sea and has wide picture
windows on three sides. Newgale House has limited windows and no sea
view. In 2014, an opportunity arose to lease the Café and its equipment for
ten years at an exceptionally good rent. However, shortly after the rental
agreement was implemented the current owner started negotiations to
purchase the Café. In the spring of 2015, Mr Carter sold the property and
the lease ceased to operate. In light of the foregoing, Mr Carter contended
that the unrealistic lease value, the fact that the lease effectively expired
within months of it starting and the total difference in use, style and
desirability indicated that the Valuation Officer was wrong to use it as a
comparable with Newgale House.

31. Mr Carter referred to Mrs Harris’ use of ‘Pebbles Café’ as a comparable
property despite the fact that it was situated at the other end of Newgale
Beach from the appeal property. He asserted that Pebbles Café had some
similarities with Sands Café in that they were of a similar size to each
other and both benefited from a beach side location. They both had large
windows and a car park was situated opposite. Despite a reduction in its
RV, Sands Café has an RV 130% greater than that of Pebbles Café for no
apparent reason. He said that “Newsurf” was hopelessly overpriced in
terMrs of its RV given the history of wave damage, road closures and
cannot be insured for flood damage. Mr Carter said that the owners of
Newsurf and Sands Café still maintain that their RV’s are excessive.

32. Mr Carter gave details regarding the fact that different caseworkers had
been assigned to deal with his case and that Mrs Harris had refused to
inspect the premises. During his discussions with the VO, the offer of RV
£14,500 with effect from 1st April 2017 had been advanced. As a corollary,
Mr Carter felt that the matter had to progress to a tribunal hearing.

33. In his summary, Mr Carter pointed out that a lease had been offered to
Gengard in respect of a property of 2000 sq ft in size and in a prime
location in Bridge Street, Haverfordwest for £10,400. It was close to a

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 8 of 10
number of well-known retail outlets such as Greggs, Specsavers and a
post office. Haverfordwest is a town that comprised a population of some
11,000 people and Bridge Street enjoyed a good level of footfall. By
contrast Newgale House which comprised some 3,000 sq ft was on a road
which might only be in existence for another six years and which suffered
from numerous closures during the winter. The area was supported by a
population of approximately 43 people. He added that the only viable
businesses in the area were those in the tourism industry. He referred to
conclusions drawn by Mr Parr on the same matter who opined that the
property would be hard to let at a value above £7,500. He said that the
uncertainty of the area’s continued existence would militate against
anyone starting a business in the area. He did not accept that the 2017
level of value should be greater than that of the 2010 level of value and
sought a value of RV £8,500 with effect from 1st April 2017.

34. At the conclusion of the hearing, the Tribunal decided to reserve its
decision.

Decision of the Tribunal

35. Having considered all of the evidence placed before it, the tribunal decided
to allow the appeal but only to the extent Mrs Harris conceded in her
valuation.

36. In making its decision, the Tribunal was mindful of Schedule 6 of the Local
Government Finance Act 1988, as amended which defined Rateable Value
and to which Mrs Harris spoke to in her advocate’s evidence.  As a
consequence of this, the Tribunal understood that in the context of a rating
valuation one had to consider and determine what rent the appeal property
could reasonably have been expected to realise had it been let on the open
market as at the 1 April 2015 - that being the antecedent valuation date for
the purposes of all entries in the 2017 Rating List. The Tribunal was also
required to bear in mind the statutory assumption one must make regarding
the terMrs of the presumed letting and the date at which various, mainly
physical factors relevant to the property and its locality, must be considered.
In this case the day on which physical matters must be contemplated (the
‘material day’) was 1st April 2017.

37. The judgment in Lotus and Delta Ltd which Mrs Harris advanced in her
evidence, provided guidance on the weight to be attached to rental and
assessment evidence.  This case also maintained that one would consider
the rent on the subject property as the correct starting point in such an
exercise. In addition, it was held that the passing rents on similar
properties could be examined where they were available as were the
assessments on comparable properties.

38. The Tribunal considered that the 1st December 2017 rent on the appeal
property was tainted as a result of an in-house connected party
arrangement and therefore carried no weight. Moreover, it transpired some
two and a half years from the AVD and this did little to inform the Tribunal

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 9 of 10
as to how reflective it was of open market values that prevailed at that
time. As a consequence, the Tribunal was not convinced by the appellant’s
rationale for using a rent such as this in these proceedings.

39. The Tribunal was not persuaded that the November 2014 rent of Sands
Café should be regarded as unrealistic as Mr Carter had described it in his
evidence. The reason for this was because the rental value for this
property was  struck between unconnected parties some 5 months prior to
the AVD. The Tribunal did not consider the fact that the property was
subsequently sold in 2015 invalidated the usefulness of this piece of
evidence.

40. The Tribunal attached little weight to the evidence contained in Mr Parr’s
February 2017 letter because it related to an earlier appeal that Mr Carter
had made in respect of the appeal property’s 2010 Rating List valuation.
Mr Carter had not persuaded the Tribunal that the relevance of particulars
of properties situated elsewhere in Haverfordwest and its environs and
cited in this schedule of evidence bore any relevance to the issues now
under consideration.

41. The Tribunal observed that Sands café and Pebbles at Chapel Farm had
certain physical characteristics that were arguably superior to those at
Newgale House. Both comparable properties benefitted from larger
windows, car park and beach side access. However, the Tribunal had
noted during the cross-examination of evidence, that Sands enjoyed an A3
class of use which the Tribunal deduced may have made the property
more desirable. Moreover, the appeal property’s underlying level of value
of £55/m2 was considerably lower than these properties and, in the
absence of more compelling evidence, it was difficult for the Tribunal to
conclude that the Valuation Officer’s revised valuation of the subject
property was unreasonable.

42. Mr Carter contended that owing to ecological factors, commercial viability
in Newgale could only be sustained for a finite period of time. The Tribunal
understood that the local authority had made proposals about how to
manage the effects of the sea on Newgale but apart from some
exploratory works which were undertaken after the 2017 list came into
force, nothing physical had taken place in the area. With this in mind, one
had to take account of the physical nature of the appeal property and of
the area in which it was situated on the material day, which in this case
was 1st April 2017. Should the area be subject to a future material change
in circuMrstances then such matters could be reflected in a separate
proposal, but this appeal could not reflect circuMrstances that had yet to
take place.

43. The Tribunal appreciated Mr Carter’s obvious frustration that several
different caseworkers had been assigned to this case. However, this was
not a matter that fell into the Tribunal’s jurisdiction, nor did it feel that
comments about this would be appropriate to make within the scope of this
appeal.

Non-Domestic Rating Appeal

Page 10 of 10

44. Although the Tribunal understood that Mr Sanderson remained concerned
with the level of value he had agreed with the Valuation Officer in respect
of Sands Café and Newsurf, there was no avenue, for the reasons Mrs
Harris spoke to in her case, for redress here. Even if the motivation for him
saying this was to assist the appellant in his case, such comments were
without foundation and therefore attracted  little weight.

45. Whilst the Tribunal accepted that the circuMrstances at Newgale were
unique, one must also reflect on the fact that this area is renown as an
area of outstanding natural beauty as well as highly regarded by water
sport/leisure enthusiasts. Mr Carter maintained the view of his appointed
representative that no one would pay more than £7,500 per annum in rent,
yet the Tribunal had observed that the operator of Sands Café had done
precisely that only a matter of months prior to the AVD. There was no
evidence before the Tribunal which suggested that if vacant and to let at
the AVD, the appeal property being significantly larger property would
command a rent less than that actually achieved for Sands Café.  Mr
Carter suggested the underlying level should be half that proposed by the
Valuation Officer. However, he had not, in the Tribunal’s opinion produced
evidence of sufficient strength that supported that contention. As a
corollary, the Tribunal was not prepared to revise the compiled list entry
beyond that conceded by the Valuation Officer in this case.

46. The parties are entitled to appeal to the Upper Chamber of the Lands
Tribunal within 28 days of the date of this decision. In making its decision,
the Tribunal orders the Valuation Officer to amend the 2017 Rating List to
accord with this decision.
